title: On the Face of It
summary: Susan Hill's play presents a meeting between Derry, a teenage boy with a burnt face who has withdrawn from the world, and Mr Lamb, an old man with a tin leg who lives with openness and hope. Their conversation changes the boy's attitude to himself and to life.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Susan Hill (born 1942) is an English novelist and playwright. Her work often explores loneliness, loss and the inner lives of people set apart from others.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Derry, fourteen, climbs into Mr Lamb's garden thinking it is empty. One side of his face was burnt by acid, and he believes everyone fears and pities him. Mr Lamb, who lost a leg in the war, talks to him without horror or pity and shows him another way of seeing the world. Derry goes home, then defies his mother to return, only to find the old man lying on the ground after a fall from his ladder.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
• Scene one, the meeting: Derry is startled when Mr Lamb speaks to him and wants to leave. Lamb tells him he is welcome: the gate is always open, and he is fond of anyone who comes in.
  • Derry's bitterness: He says people stare at his face and are afraid. He has overheard hurtful remarks, including a woman saying that only a mother could love such a face, and relatives saying he should be with others 'like him'.
  • Lamb's way of seeing: He points to plants others call weeds and says it is only a name; all are living, growing things. He hears bees not as buzzing but as singing. Children call him 'Lamey-Lamb', but he does not let it trouble him. He reminds Derry that he still has two arms, two legs, eyes, ears, a tongue and a brain, and can achieve what he sets his mind to.
  • The man in the locked room: Lamb tells of a man so afraid of everything that he shut himself in his room, and died when a picture fell on his head. Hiding from life is no protection.
  • A change begins: Derry is curious about the house without curtains, the crab apples to be picked for jelly and Lamb's 'hundreds' of friends. He offers to help and runs home to tell his mother.
  • Scene two: His mother has heard unkind talk about Mr Lamb and forbids him to go back. Derry insists that the old man says things nobody else has said, things that matter, and that if he does not return he will never go anywhere again.
  • The ending: Meanwhile Lamb climbs the ladder to pick the apples and falls with it. Derry arrives to find him motionless and weeps, begging him to get up. The ending is tragic, yet Derry has already been changed.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Physical impairment and social attitudes: the pain of a disability is made worse by people's stares, pity and rejection.
  • Loneliness and alienation: both characters are lonely, but they respond differently.
  • Optimism versus pessimism: attitude, not appearance, decides the quality of life.
  • Appearance and reality: what a person is 'on the face of it' is not who they truly are.
  • Acceptance and human connection: one understanding listener can restore confidence.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Derry: sensitive, intelligent and observant, but bitter, suspicious and withdrawn. He has low self-esteem and expects rejection. He is nevertheless honest and willing to listen, and by the end he has the courage to defy his mother and act on his own decision.

Mr Lamb: an old, lonely man with an artificial leg, yet cheerful, patient, wise and open-hearted. He loves nature, books and people, keeps his gate and windows open, and never complains. Beneath his cheer lies a hint of sadness, for he knows that visitors seldom return.

Derry's mother: protective and anxious; she loves him but, by shielding him and distrusting others, keeps him isolated.

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The title is an idiom meaning 'judging by appearances'. It also points literally to Derry's face. The play shows that judging by the surface is misleading: a scarred face hides a thoughtful boy, and a lame old man is rich in spirit. Its message is that people with disabilities need acceptance and respect rather than pity, and that one's own outlook can turn a handicap into strength.

keyTerms.definition: An idiom meaning 'as it appears on the surface, before the facts are known'.
Small, sour wild apples, used for making jelly.
An artificial leg; Mr Lamb's real leg was blown off in the war.
The feeling of being cut off from other people or from society.
A hopeful attitude that expects good outcomes.
The opinion a person holds of their own worth.

mcqs.q: How did Derry's face get burnt?
mcqs.explanation: Acid ate away one side of his face.

mcqs.q: How did Mr Lamb lose his leg?
options: In a fall from a tree
It was blown off in the war
mcqs.explanation: He lost it in the war and now has a tin leg.

mcqs.q: What does Mr Lamb say about the sound of bees?
mcqs.explanation: Where others hear buzzing, he hears singing: the difference is in outlook.

mcqs.q: The story of the man who locked himself in his room teaches that
options: shutting oneself away from life is useless
mcqs.explanation: He died anyway; fear and withdrawal do not protect anyone.

mcqs.q: Why does Derry's mother not want him to visit Mr Lamb?
options: She has heard unfavourable things about him
mcqs.explanation: She relies on gossip and is over-protective.

mcqs.q: What does Mr Lamb's open gate and curtainless window symbolise?
options: Openness to people and to life
mcqs.explanation: He shuts nothing and no one out.

mcqs.q: What happens to Mr Lamb at the end?
options: He falls from the ladder while picking crab apples
He goes to hospital for his leg
mcqs.explanation: The ladder topples and he falls; Derry finds him lying still.

options: The physical pain of the burn
People's attitude of fear and pity towards him
mcqs.explanation: The stares and remarks of others wound him more than the injury.

questions.q: Why does Derry go into Mr Lamb's garden, and why does he want to leave at once?
questions.answerHtml: He climbs the wall believing the place to be empty, seeking solitude. When Mr Lamb speaks, he is startled and wants to go because he expects the old man, like everyone else, to be repelled by his face.

questions.q: How does Mr Lamb's attitude to his own disability differ from Derry's?
questions.answerHtml: Derry is ashamed and angry and hides from people. Mr Lamb accepts his tin leg calmly, ignores the children's teasing and keeps himself busy with his garden, books and visitors. He refuses to let the handicap define his life.

questions.q: Why does Derry go back to Mr Lamb in the end?
questions.answerHtml: Mr Lamb treated him as a normal person and said things that mattered, which no one had said before. Derry feels that if he does not return he will never go anywhere again; going back is his first step out of isolation.

questions.q: The actual pain caused by a physical impairment is often much less than the sense of alienation felt by the person. Discuss with reference to the play.
questions.answerHtml:
Derry's burn has healed; it is the behaviour of people that keeps the wound open. He notices their frightened looks and overhears remarks suggesting that he is ugly and should live apart with others like him. Even kindness feels like pity. As a result he avoids company and trusts no one.

Mr Lamb has faced the same thing. Children mock his limp and few visitors come twice. Yet he does not withdraw. He keeps his gate open, welcomes whoever enters and finds companionship in nature. He shows that alienation deepens when a person accepts society's verdict.

The play thus suggests that the disabled need acceptance rather than sympathy. A scar or a missing limb limits a person far less than rejection does. Mr Lamb heals Derry not with medicine but by treating him as an equal, which gives the boy the confidence that years of protection had failed to give.

questions.q: How does Mr Lamb bring about a change in Derry?
questions.answerHtml:
Mr Lamb begins by not reacting to Derry's face. He neither stares nor looks away, and he speaks to him as he would to anyone. This alone surprises the boy.

He then offers a new way of looking at things. A weed and a flower are both growing plants; buzzing can be heard as singing; a handicap is only one fact about a person. He reminds Derry of all the abilities he still has and tells him that he can do better than others if he chooses. Through the story of the man who hid in his room and died anyway, he shows that fear and hatred harm more than any acid.

He also gives Derry a purpose by inviting him to help pick the crab apples. Gradually Derry's hostility turns into curiosity and then attachment. In the last scene he opposes his mother and runs back. Although he finds the old man fallen, the change is complete: Derry has learnt to face the world on his own terms.
